questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

schema.name: Glob
schema.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

schema.name: Grep
schema.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

The smoke test passed: both workspaces reported connected in a Windows notification, so phase 0.5 is done.

**What changed**
- In [docs/PLAN.md](docs/PLAN.md), phase 0.5 is ticked with a line saying both runs reported connected. The status line now reads "phases 0 and 0.5 done. Next: phase 1 spikes."
- That edit isn't committed yet. Neither are the ⋯ menu edits to [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) and [README.md](README.md). All three would go into one commit.

**Before pushing**
The Entire remote (`origin`) has no branches yet. Git shows `main`'s link to `origin/main` as gone. If only `plugin-scaffold` is pushed, it would be the first branch there and could become the remote's default. Pushing `main` first would make `main` the default. All seven commits on `plugin-scaffold` would go up, and Entire syncs their checkpoints as part of the push.

**A small fix for later**
Orca adds the plugin id to the front of every notification title, so ours shows as `petercr.entire: Entire: connected`. We could drop our own "Entire: " prefix, which would also save a reinstall cycle later.

files.content:
# Entire for Orca

An Orca plugin (trusted-worker) that brings Entire trails, findings and checkpoints into Orca. Read
[docs/PLAN.md](docs/PLAN.md) first: it covers the environment, what Orca's plugin API allows, the spike
results, the architecture, the phases and what we have asked the Orca team for.

## Layout

- `orca-plugin.json`: the manifest (format 2, host API 1). After changing it, validate it against

# Orca plugin host API reference

<!-- Generated by `pnpm generate:plugin-schemas` from src/shared/plugins. Do not edit. -->

Host API 1.0 (`"pluginApi": 1`). Workers call a method with `await orca.host.call(name, params)`; panels and custom editors call the same methods through `window.orca.host.call(name, params)`. Each method lists the surfaces allowed to call it; any other surface gets `not_permitted`. `orca.host.has(name)` answers synchronously whether this Orca offers a method on the current surface, and `orca.api` is `{ major, minor }`. See [Plugin authoring](./plugin-authoring.md) for the frame API.

Every call is checked against the capabilities the user approved, and params are validated before Orca runs anything: params are strict, so a field this Orca does not know is refused with `invalid_params` instead of being dropped. Mutations are recorded in the audit log as `plugin:<publisher>.<id>`.

## Methods

| Method | Capability | Surfaces | Mutation | Since | Summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`workspace.readContext`](#workspacereadcontext) | `workspace:read` | worker, panel, editor | no | 1.0 | Branch, name and terminal ids of the focused workspace, or null when none is focused. |
| [`terminal.sendText`](#terminalsendtext) | `terminal:send` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Types text into one terminal named by id, optionally pressing Enter. |
| [`notifications.show`](#notificationsshow) | `notifications:show` | worker, panel, editor | yes | 1.0 | Shows a desktop notification. |
| [`storage.get`](#storageget) | `storage:own` | worker | no | 1.0 | Reads a JSON value from the plugin's private store; null when absent. |
| [`storage.set`](#storageset) | `storage:own` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Writes a JSON value to the plugin's private store. |
| [`storage.delete`](#storagedelete) | `storage:own` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Removes a key from the plugin's private store. |
| [`storage.keys`](#storagekeys) | `storage:own` | worker | no | 1.0 | Lists the keys in the plugin's private store. |
| [`secrets.get`](#secretsget) | `secrets:own` | worker | no | 1.0 | Reads a secret from the plugin's encrypted secrets file; null when absent. |
| [`secrets.set`](#secretsset) | `secrets:own` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Stores a secret in the plugin's encrypted secrets file. |
| [`secrets.delete`](#secretsdelete) | `secrets:own` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Removes a secret from the plugin's encrypted secrets file. |
| [`settings.get`](#settingsget) | `settings:own` | worker | no | 1.0 | Reads every setting the plugin owns. |
| [`settings.set`](#settingsset) | `settings:own` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Writes one setting the plugin owns. |

### `workspace.readContext`

Branch, name and terminal ids of the focused workspace, or null when none is focused.

```ts
(params: {}) => { branch: string; displayName: string; terminals: { id: string }[] } | null
```

### `terminal.sendText`

Types text into one terminal named by id, optionally pressing Enter.

```ts
(params: { terminalId: string; text: string; enter?: boolean }) => { accepted: boolean }
```

### `notifications.show`

Shows a desktop notification.

```ts
(params: { title: string; body?: string }) => { delivered: boolean }
```

### `storage.get`

Reads a JSON value from the plugin's private store; null when absent.

```ts
(params: { key: string }) => { value: JSON }
```

### `storage.set`

Writes a JSON value to the plugin's private store.

```ts
(params: { key: string; value: JSON }) => { ok: true }
```

### `storage.delete`

Removes a key from the plugin's private store.

```ts
(params: { key: string }) => { ok: true }
```

### `storage.keys`

Lists the keys in the plugin's private store.

```ts
(params: {}) => { keys: string[] }
```

### `secrets.get`

Reads a secret from the plugin's encrypted secrets file; null when absent.

```ts
(params: { key: string }) => { value: string | null }
```

### `secrets.set`

Stores a secret in the plugin's encrypted secrets file.

```ts
(params: { key: string; value: string }) => { ok: true }
```

### `secrets.delete`

Removes a secret from the plugin's encrypted secrets file.

```ts
(params: { key: string }) => { ok: true }
```

### `settings.get`

Reads every setting the plugin owns.

```ts
(params: {}) => { settings: Record<string, JSON> }
```

### `settings.set`

Writes one setting the plugin owns.

```ts
(params: { key: string; value: JSON }) => { ok: true }
```

## Errors

A failed call rejects with an `Error` carrying `code`, `message`, `retryable` and, for `rate_limited`, `retryAfterMs`. Treat a code not listed here as `action_failed`:

- `invalid_request`: the call itself is malformed.
- `invalid_params`: params do not match the method, including a field this Orca does not know; the message names it.
- `unknown_method`: the method does not exist in this Orca.
- `capability_denied`: the manifest does not declare the capability.
- `consent_required`: the plugin is disabled or the user has not approved this version.
- `not_permitted`: the method or document is not available here, e.g. a worker-only method from a panel.
- `rate_limited`: calls arrive faster than the budget; `retryAfterMs` says when to try again.
- `unavailable`: the service behind the method is not running yet.
- `action_failed`: the method ran and failed.
- `cancelled`: the caller aborted the call through its `signal`.
- `timeout`: Orca gave up waiting.
- `conflict`: the call was made against a stale version, e.g. an editor edit after an outside change.
- `too_large`: the message is larger than Orca accepts.

## Stability and deprecation

Plugins are in Alpha: the manifest v2 format and catalog format are stable contracts; items listed as experimental in [Plugin authoring](./plugin-authoring.md#stability) may change.

- **Host API 1 is frozen.** Within `pluginApi` 1, methods, params and results only grow: a new method or a new optional param arrives with a higher `Since` minor, and nothing listed here is removed, renamed or narrowed.
- **Deprecation.** A method to be retired is marked deprecated in this table and keeps working for the rest of the major.
- **New majors.** A breaking change ships as a new `pluginApi` major beside the old one. Orca refuses a manifest whose `pluginApi` names a major it does not implement, with "update Orca", instead of loading it against the wrong API.
- **Detect, do not assume.** Check `orca.host.has(name)` or `orca.api.minor` before calling a method newer than the oldest Orca you support; a call that slips through fails with `unknown_method`.

1	# Writing an Orca plugin
2	
3	From an empty folder to a plugin anyone can install from a catalog. The field-by-field rules
4	live in the generated references: [manifest](plugin-manifest.md), [catalog](plugin-catalog.md),
5	[host API](plugin-host-api.md), [themes](plugin-themes.md) and [theme tokens](plugin-theme-tokens.md),
6	[syntaxes](plugin-syntax.md).
7	
8	## 1. Write
9	
10	A plugin is a folder (in practice its own Git repository) with `orca-plugin.json` at the root.
11	Start from `examples/plugins/orca-gleam-syntax`, which carries the JSON Schema for editor
12	completion, or from one of:
13	
14	| Example                              | Execution        | Shows                                |
15	| ------------------------------------ | ---------------- | ------------------------------------ |
16	| `examples/plugins/orca-gleam-syntax` | `data`           | A syntax, no code                    |
17	| `examples/plugins/hello-orca`        | `trusted-worker` | A panel, a worker command and events |
18	
19	Set `publisher` to the GitHub or GitLab user or organization that owns your repository (`acme`
20	for `github.com/acme/gleam-syntax`), or the official and community catalogs reject the listing.
21	When copying the Gleam example, also drop its `stablyai` publisher and `orca-` id prefix: both are
22	reserved for Orca's own plugins.
23	
24	Pick the lowest `execution` profile that covers what you contribute; it decides what the user is
25	asked to approve:
26	
27	- `data`: themes, terminal themes, icon themes, syntaxes, translations. Installs in one click.
28	- `declarative`: commands that run Orca actions, shortcuts, VM recipes. Reviewed before they
29	  are enabled.
30	- `sandboxed-ui`: panels and custom editors, in a sandboxed frame that talks to Orca only
31	  through `window.orca` (see [Frames](#frames-windoworca)) and can call only the host methods
32	  whose surfaces list `panel` or `editor`.
33	  Orca's colors reach frame CSS as `--orca-background`, `--orca-foreground`, `--orca-primary`
34	  and the rest of its panel token set, so they never collide with a frame's own variables.
35	- `trusted-worker`: `main` runs in a separate Node process and can call every host method its
36	  `capabilities` allow. There is no global switch for these full-access plugins: each one runs
37	  only after the user approves it on install. An enterprise policy to block full-access plugins
38	  may come later.
39	
40	Set `engines.orca` to the newest `Since` of any field you use, and `pluginApi` (currently `1`)
41	only when a panel or worker calls the host API.
42	
43	### Frames: `window.orca`
44	
45	Before any plugin code runs, the frame shell defines a frozen `window.orca`. It is the only
46	supported way to talk to Orca; the messages underneath are internal and change without notice.
47	
48	```js
49	orca.api // { major: 1, minor: 0 }: the host API this Orca implements
50	if (orca.host.has('workspace.readContext')) {
51	  // Synchronous: is the method offered to this surface by this Orca?
52	  const controller = new AbortController()
53	  try {
54	    const context = await orca.host.call('workspace.readContext', {}, { signal: controller.signal })
55	  } catch (error) {
56	    // error.code, error.message, error.retryable, error.retryAfterMs (rate_limited only)
57	  }
58	}
59	const subscription = orca.on('theme', ({ colorScheme }) => {})
60	subscription.dispose()
61	```
62	
63	Methods, their surfaces and their errors are in the [host API reference](plugin-host-api.md).
64	Aborting the `signal` rejects the call with `cancelled`. Treat an error `code` you do not know as
65	`action_failed`. Params are strict: a field the running Orca does not know is refused with
66	`invalid_params`, so check `orca.host.has` or `orca.api.minor` before using a newer one.
67	
68	Workers get the same calls on the `orca` object passed to `activate(orca)`:
69	`orca.api`, `orca.host.call(method, params, { signal })`, `orca.host.has(method)`, plus
70	`orca.commands.register(id, (args, { signal }) => …)` and `orca.events.on(event, handler)`, which
71	both return `{ dispose() }`. A command's `signal` aborts when Orca stops waiting for it. In
72	`agent.status.changed`, `state` and `mainAgent.state` are one of `working`, `blocked`, `waiting`
73	and `done`.
74	
75	### Custom editors
76	
77	A custom editor opens files that end in one of its `extensions` (with the dot, such as
78	`.excalidraw`) or carry one of its exact `filenames` in the editor tab, beside Source. Syntaxes
79	match files the same way. It runs in the same sandboxed frame as a panel (no Node, no file system), and Orca keeps
80	the buffer, dirty state, saving, the external-change banner, read-only tabs and remote (SSH or
81	paired host) files; the frame only gets the document, never a path. Editor and panel plugins are
82	trusted code, and an editor can read every file it opens, so install ones you trust.
83	
84	An editor's `window.orca` adds `document`:
85	
86	```js
87	const doc = await orca.document.get() // { version, readOnly, content, fileType? }
88	// The current document right away, then each one Orca sends when the file changes outside the editor.
89	orca.document.onDidChange((doc) => render(doc))
90	await orca.document.applyEdit({ baseVersion: doc.version, content: { kind: 'text', text } })
91	orca.on('editor.flush', () => sendPendingEdit()) // before a save; Orca waits for the promise
92	```
93	
94	`content` is `{ kind: 'text', text }` for a text editor (the default `contentKind`). An edit is
95	the full new content, made against document `baseVersion`; send one only when the user changes
96	the document, never on load. `applyEdit` rejects with `conflict` when the file changed outside
97	the editor since that version (edit the newer document instead), `too_large` past the size cap,
98	and `not_permitted` when `readOnly` is true (an agent transcript, say). `version` rises with each
99	document Orca sends, not with your own edits.
100	
101	Set `"contentKind": "bytes"` for a binary format such as a spreadsheet. Orca reads the file
102	itself (locally, over SSH or from a paired host) and the document's `content` is
103	`{ kind: 'bytes', bytes }`, where `bytes` is an `ArrayBuffer`, plus the matched suffix as
104	`fileType`. An edit is the whole new file the same way: `content: { kind: 'bytes', bytes }`.
105	Orca marks the tab dirty and saves the bytes with the tab's normal save, replacing the file
106	atomically; a save is refused if the file changed on disk since the document's version, and the
107	banner offers Reload or Overwrite. Saving to a remote host needs an Orca server new enough to
108	replace binary files. Source shows the binary placeholder, unsaved bytes are not kept across
109	restarts, and bytes tabs don't autosave.
110	
111	Documents and edits are capped at 64 MiB, text or bytes, on every route (local, SSH and paired
112	hosts): a larger file shows "too large to open", and a larger edit is rejected with `too_large`.
113	Past 16 MiB the tab notes that the file may take a moment. Orca saves on its own save shortcut pressed
114	inside the frame, never on a call alone.
115	
116	Theme changes do not reload the frame: the shell updates the `--orca-*` variables and the
117	`light`/`dark` class on `<html>` in place and emits `theme`. Restyle from the variables, or
118	listen with `orca.on('theme', …)`, to follow it.
119	
120	## 2. Load it while you work
121	
122	1. Settings → Plugins: click **Turn on plugins**.
123	2. **Development folders…** → add the plugin folder. A development folder overrides an installed
124	   copy with the same `<publisher>.<id>`.
125	3. Review and enable it. Nothing runs before that.
126	
127	Orca watches development folders and reloads the plugin when its manifest or files change.
128	Theme, syntax and translation edits show up as you save. Panels and workers are not bound to
129	their files in development, so saving does not ask for approval again; adding a capability or
130	moving to a higher execution profile does. Shortcuts and recipes are tied to their files, so
131	each change to them is reviewed again. Use **Restart** on the plugin row after changing a
132	worker, and the plugin's logs to see what it printed.
133	
134	## 3. Validate
135	
136	```sh
137	pnpm validate:plugin path/to/plugin
138	```
139	
140	This runs the manifest checks Orca runs, strictly: unknown keys, limits, contributions beyond the
141	execution profile, and an `engines.orca` too low for the fields used. On a catalog it also
142	checks that listed images exist and fit. In a Git repository it warns when `publisher` is not the
143	owner of the `origin` remote. Run it in CI for the plugin and catalog repositories.
144	
145	## 4. Publish to a catalog
146	
147	A catalog is a Git repository with `orca-catalog.json` at its root that lists plugins and pins
148	each release to an exact commit and file hash, so Orca refuses bytes the catalog did not vouch
149	for.
150	
151	1. Commit the plugin and run `pnpm validate:plugin` on its directory. It prints the
152	   release entry for `HEAD`: version, full commit SHA, `contentHash`, execution profile, minimum
153	   Orca, contribution summary, capabilities and file types. Every field must match
154	   what Orca finds at install, so paste it rather than writing it by hand.
155	2. Add or update the plugin's entry in the catalog's `orca-catalog.json`, newest release first:
156	
157	   ```json

# Writing an Orca plugin

From an empty folder to a plugin anyone can install from a catalog. The field-by-field rules
live in the generated references: [manifest](plugin-manifest.md), [catalog](plugin-catalog.md),
[host API](plugin-host-api.md), [themes](plugin-themes.md) and [theme tokens](plugin-theme-tokens.md),
[syntaxes](plugin-syntax.md).

## 1. Write

A plugin is a folder (in practice its own Git repository) with `orca-plugin.json` at the root.
Start from `examples/plugins/orca-gleam-syntax`, which carries the JSON Schema for editor
completion, or from one of:

| Example                              | Execution        | Shows                                |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `examples/plugins/orca-gleam-syntax` | `data`           | A syntax, no code                    |
| `examples/plugins/hello-orca`        | `trusted-worker` | A panel, a worker command and events |

Set `publisher` to the GitHub or GitLab user or organization that owns your repository (`acme`
for `github.com/acme/gleam-syntax`), or the official and community catalogs reject the listing.
When copying the Gleam example, also drop its `stablyai` publisher and `orca-` id prefix: both are
reserved for Orca's own plugins.

Pick the lowest `execution` profile that covers what you contribute; it decides what the user is
asked to approve:

- `data`: themes, terminal themes, icon themes, syntaxes, translations. Installs in one click.
- `declarative`: commands that run Orca actions, shortcuts, VM recipes. Reviewed before they
  are enabled.
- `sandboxed-ui`: panels and custom editors, in a sandboxed frame that talks to Orca only
  through `window.orca` (see [Frames](#frames-windoworca)) and can call only the host methods
  whose surfaces list `panel` or `editor`.
  Orca's colors reach frame CSS as `--orca-background`, `--orca-foreground`, `--orca-primary`
  and the rest of its panel token set, so they never collide with a frame's own variables.
- `trusted-worker`: `main` runs in a separate Node process and can call every host method its
  `capabilities` allow. There is no global switch for these full-access plugins: each one runs
  only after the user approves it on install. An enterprise policy to block full-access plugins
  may come later.

Set `engines.orca` to the newest `Since` of any field you use, and `pluginApi` (currently `1`)
only when a panel or worker calls the host API.

### Frames: `window.orca`

Before any plugin code runs, the frame shell defines a frozen `window.orca`. It is the only
supported way to talk to Orca; the messages underneath are internal and change without notice.

```js
orca.api // { major: 1, minor: 0 }: the host API this Orca implements
if (orca.host.has('workspace.readContext')) {
  // Synchronous: is the method offered to this surface by this Orca?
  const controller = new AbortController()
  try {
    const context = await orca.host.call('workspace.readContext', {}, { signal: controller.signal })
  } catch (error) {
    // error.code, error.message, error.retryable, error.retryAfterMs (rate_limited only)
  }
}
const subscription = orca.on('theme', ({ colorScheme }) => {})
subscription.dispose()
```

Methods, their surfaces and their errors are in the [host API reference](plugin-host-api.md).
Aborting the `signal` rejects the call with `cancelled`. Treat an error `code` you do not know as
`action_failed`. Params are strict: a field the running Orca does not know is refused with
`invalid_params`, so check `orca.host.has` or `orca.api.minor` before using a newer one.

Workers get the same calls on the `orca` object passed to `activate(orca)`:
`orca.api`, `orca.host.call(method, params, { signal })`, `orca.host.has(method)`, plus
`orca.commands.register(id, (args, { signal }) => …)` and `orca.events.on(event, handler)`, which
both return `{ dispose() }`. A command's `signal` aborts when Orca stops waiting for it. In
`agent.status.changed`, `state` and `mainAgent.state` are one of `working`, `blocked`, `waiting`
and `done`.

### Custom editors

A custom editor opens files that end in one of its `extensions` (with the dot, such as
`.excalidraw`) or carry one of its exact `filenames` in the editor tab, beside Source. Syntaxes
match files the same way. It runs in the same sandboxed frame as a panel (no Node, no file system), and Orca keeps
the buffer, dirty state, saving, the external-change banner, read-only tabs and remote (SSH or
paired host) files; the frame only gets the document, never a path. Editor and panel plugins are
trusted code, and an editor can read every file it opens, so install ones you trust.

An editor's `window.orca` adds `document`:

```js
const doc = await orca.document.get() // { version, readOnly, content, fileType? }
// The current document right away, then each one Orca sends when the file changes outside the editor.
orca.document.onDidChange((doc) => render(doc))
await orca.document.applyEdit({ baseVersion: doc.version, content: { kind: 'text', text } })
orca.on('editor.flush', () => sendPendingEdit()) // before a save; Orca waits for the promise
```

`content` is `{ kind: 'text', text }` for a text editor (the default `contentKind`). An edit is
the full new content, made against document `baseVersion`; send one only when the user changes
the document, never on load. `applyEdit` rejects with `conflict` when the file changed outside
the editor since that version (edit the newer document instead), `too_large` past the size cap,
and `not_permitted` when `readOnly` is true (an agent transcript, say). `version` rises with each
document Orca sends, not with your own edits.

Set `"contentKind": "bytes"` for a binary format such as a spreadsheet. Orca reads the file
itself (locally, over SSH or from a paired host) and the document's `content` is
`{ kind: 'bytes', bytes }`, where `bytes` is an `ArrayBuffer`, plus the matched suffix as
`fileType`. An edit is the whole new file the same way: `content: { kind: 'bytes', bytes }`.
Orca marks the tab dirty and saves the bytes with the tab's normal save, replacing the file
atomically; a save is refused if the file changed on disk since the document's version, and the
banner offers Reload or Overwrite. Saving to a remote host needs an Orca server new enough to
replace binary files. Source shows the binary placeholder, unsaved bytes are not kept across
restarts, and bytes tabs don't autosave.

Documents and edits are capped at 64 MiB, text or bytes, on every route (local, SSH and paired
hosts): a larger file shows "too large to open", and a larger edit is rejected with `too_large`.
Past 16 MiB the tab notes that the file may take a moment. Orca saves on its own save shortcut pressed
inside the frame, never on a call alone.

Theme changes do not reload the frame: the shell updates the `--orca-*` variables and the
`light`/`dark` class on `<html>` in place and emits `theme`. Restyle from the variables, or
listen with `orca.on('theme', …)`, to follow it.

## 2. Load it while you work

1. Settings → Plugins: click **Turn on plugins**.
2. **Development folders…** → add the plugin folder. A development folder overrides an installed
   copy with the same `<publisher>.<id>`.
3. Review and enable it. Nothing runs before that.

Orca watches development folders and reloads the plugin when its manifest or files change.
Theme, syntax and translation edits show up as you save. Panels and workers are not bound to
their files in development, so saving does not ask for approval again; adding a capability or
moving to a higher execution profile does. Shortcuts and recipes are tied to their files, so
each change to them is reviewed again. Use **Restart** on the plugin row after changing a
worker, and the plugin's logs to see what it printed.

## 3. Validate

```sh
pnpm validate:plugin path/to/plugin
```

This runs the manifest checks Orca runs, strictly: unknown keys, limits, contributions beyond the
execution profile, and an `engines.orca` too low for the fields used. On a catalog it also
checks that listed images exist and fit. In a Git repository it warns when `publisher` is not the
owner of the `origin` remote. Run it in CI for the plugin and catalog repositories.

## 4. Publish to a catalog

A catalog is a Git repository with `orca-catalog.json` at its root that lists plugins and pins
each release to an exact commit and file hash, so Orca refuses bytes the catalog did not vouch
for.

1. Commit the plugin and run `pnpm validate:plugin` on its directory. It prints the
   release entry for `HEAD`: version, full commit SHA, `contentHash`, execution profile, minimum
   Orca, contribution summary, capabilities and file types. Every field must match
   what Orca finds at install, so paste it rather than writing it by hand.
2. Add or update the plugin's entry in the catalog's `orca-catalog.json`, newest release first:

   ```json
   {
     "id": "acme.gleam-syntax",
     "source": {
       "kind": "git",
       "url": "https://github.com/acme/orca-gleam-syntax.git",
       "ref": "main"
     },
     "categories": ["languages"],
     "releases": [{ "...": "the printed entry" }]
   }
   ```

   `commit` must be a full 40-character SHA. A tag or branch name is refused by validation and
   skipped by Orca. Keep the previous release listed when you raise `engines.orca`, so older
   Orca still has something to install.

   **One repository can hold many plugins.** Put each in its own directory, such as
   `plugins/gleam-syntax/orca-plugin.json`, and add `"path": "plugins/gleam-syntax"` to its
   `source`; validating that directory prints the `path` to use. Orca installs only that
   directory, and its `contentHash` covers only its files, so commits to sibling plugins never
   change it. Moving a plugin to another directory counts as a different repository.

3. Run `pnpm validate:plugin path/to/catalog` and regenerate the older
   `orca-marketplace.json` as described in the [catalog reference](plugin-catalog.md#clients-before-format-2).
4. Users add the catalog under Settings → Plugins → ⋯ → **Catalog sources…** with its Git URL and ref.

Users approve a plugin once per level of access. An update from the same repository that asks
for nothing new, code changes included, installs without asking again and stays enabled. Orca
asks again, listing what is new, when an update adds a capability, raises the execution profile,
adds a command, shortcut, panel or event subscription, ships virtual machine recipes, or comes from
a different repository.

With **Update plugins automatically** on (the default), Orca installs such updates for enabled
catalog plugins by itself, checking at startup and every 6 hours. A release installs only once it
has been listed for 12 hours, or at once from the official catalog, so a takedown has time to land.
Only pinned catalog releases (a `releases` entry with its commit and content hash) install by
themselves; a listing without one updates only when the user clicks Update. This includes
full-access plugins: an update that asks for nothing new runs its new code with the access the user
already granted, the same way an editor's extensions update. Turn the setting off to review every
update. An update that needs approval is not installed: the current version keeps running and the
plugin shows **Update needs review**.

## Planned contribution points

These `contributes` keys are reserved: a manifest may list them only as empty arrays until
their format ships. Each is planned as declared data that Orca renders and enforces, not
arbitrary plugin UI:

- `taskSources`: issue and task providers such as Asana, Linear or Jira, filled by a worker.
- `connections`: account providers with a host-run sign-in.
- `agentHarnesses`: new coding-agent harnesses described as data.
- `statusBarItems`: declarative status bar widgets whose values a worker updates.
- `sidebarCards`: declarative left-sidebar cards whose values a worker updates.
- `mcpServers`: MCP server definitions offered to the agents Orca launches.
- `skills`: agent skills shipped as files.
- `hooks`: agent lifecycle hooks for the agents Orca launches.
- `settings`: typed plugin settings shown in Orca's settings UI.

`skills`, `mcpServers` and `hooks` will mean what they mean in agent-plugin formats such as
Claude Code's. Orca does not reserve `agents`, because those formats use it for subagent files.

See [the manifest reference](plugin-manifest.md#planned-contribution-points) for details.

## Stability

Plugins are in Alpha: the manifest v2 format and catalog format are stable contracts; items
listed as experimental may change. These parts are stable and change only additively:

- manifest format 2, capability names and execution profiles;
- host API 1 (`"pluginApi": 1`): method names, params, results, surfaces and error codes;
- the frame API `window.orca` (`api`, `host.call`, `host.has`, `on`, and `document` in custom
  editors) and the document `version`/`content` shape;
- theme token names, and theme ids once published (users' settings store them);
- catalog format 2 (`orca-catalog.json`).

Experimental; these may still change without a new format:

- the `agent.status.changed` payload: `paneKey` is not yet a terminal id `terminal.sendText`
  accepts;
- the worker process model: Node version, lifecycle and the channel to Orca. Only
  `activate(orca)` and `orca.api`, `orca.host`, `orca.commands`, `orca.events` and `orca.log` are
  promised,
  and workers may be stopped at any time;
- language-pack keys, which change when Orca's source moves or its English copy changes; packs
  get best-effort coverage per release;
- `pnpm validate:plugin` output; only its exit codes (`0` valid, `1` invalid, `2` usage) are
  stable;
- `settings:own`, which stores untyped values until plugins can declare settings;
- manifest format 1, which is deprecated. Catalogs need format 2.

Data folders, `orca-plugin-image://` URLs, tab keys and the `pluginRoot` a worker receives are
internal.

1	# Orca plugin host API reference
2	
3	<!-- Generated by `pnpm generate:plugin-schemas` from src/shared/plugins. Do not edit. -->
4	
5	Host API 1.0 (`"pluginApi": 1`). Workers call a method with `await orca.host.call(name, params)`; panels and custom editors call the same methods through `window.orca.host.call(name, params)`. Each method lists the surfaces allowed to call it; any other surface gets `not_permitted`. `orca.host.has(name)` answers synchronously whether this Orca offers a method on the current surface, and `orca.api` is `{ major, minor }`. See [Plugin authoring](./plugin-authoring.md) for the frame API.
6	
7	Every call is checked against the capabilities the user approved, and params are validated before Orca runs anything: params are strict, so a field this Orca does not know is refused with `invalid_params` instead of being dropped. Mutations are recorded in the audit log as `plugin:<publisher>.<id>`.
8	
9	## Methods
10	
11	| Method | Capability | Surfaces | Mutation | Since | Summary |
12	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
13	| [`workspace.readContext`](#workspacereadcontext) | `workspace:read` | worker, panel, editor | no | 1.0 | Branch, name and terminal ids of the focused workspace, or null when none is focused. |
14	| [`terminal.sendText`](#terminalsendtext) | `terminal:send` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Types text into one terminal named by id, optionally pressing Enter. |
15	| [`notifications.show`](#notificationsshow) | `notifications:show` | worker, panel, editor | yes | 1.0 | Shows a desktop notification. |
16	| [`storage.get`](#storageget) | `storage:own` | worker | no | 1.0 | Reads a JSON value from the plugin's private store; null when absent. |
17	| [`storage.set`](#storageset) | `storage:own` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Writes a JSON value to the plugin's private store. |
18	| [`storage.delete`](#storagedelete) | `storage:own` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Removes a key from the plugin's private store. |
19	| [`storage.keys`](#storagekeys) | `storage:own` | worker | no | 1.0 | Lists the keys in the plugin's private store. |
20	| [`secrets.get`](#secretsget) | `secrets:own` | worker | no | 1.0 | Reads a secret from the plugin's encrypted secrets file; null when absent. |
21	| [`secrets.set`](#secretsset) | `secrets:own` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Stores a secret in the plugin's encrypted secrets file. |
22	| [`secrets.delete`](#secretsdelete) | `secrets:own` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Removes a secret from the plugin's encrypted secrets file. |
23	| [`settings.get`](#settingsget) | `settings:own` | worker | no | 1.0 | Reads every setting the plugin owns. |
24	| [`settings.set`](#settingsset) | `settings:own` | worker | yes | 1.0 | Writes one setting the plugin owns. |
25	
26	### `workspace.readContext`
27	
28	Branch, name and terminal ids of the focused workspace, or null when none is focused.
29	
30	```ts
31	(params: {}) => { branch: string; displayName: string; terminals: { id: string }[] } | null
32	```
33	
34	### `terminal.sendText`
35	
36	Types text into one terminal named by id, optionally pressing Enter.
37	
38	```ts
39	(params: { terminalId: string; text: string; enter?: boolean }) => { accepted: boolean }
40	```
41	
42	### `notifications.show`
43	
44	Shows a desktop notification.
45	
46	```ts
47	(params: { title: string; body?: string }) => { delivered: boolean }
48	```
49	
50	### `storage.get`
51	
52	Reads a JSON value from the plugin's private store; null when absent.
53	
54	```ts
55	(params: { key: string }) => { value: JSON }
56	```
57	
58	### `storage.set`
59	
60	Writes a JSON value to the plugin's private store.
61	
62	```ts
63	(params: { key: string; value: JSON }) => { ok: true }
64	```
65	
66	### `storage.delete`
67	
68	Removes a key from the plugin's private store.
69	
70	```ts
71	(params: { key: string }) => { ok: true }
72	```
73	
74	### `storage.keys`
75	
76	Lists the keys in the plugin's private store.
77	
78	```ts
79	(params: {}) => { keys: string[] }
80	```
81	
82	### `secrets.get`
83	
84	Reads a secret from the plugin's encrypted secrets file; null when absent.
85	
86	```ts
87	(params: { key: string }) => { value: string | null }
88	```
89	
90	### `secrets.set`
91	
92	Stores a secret in the plugin's encrypted secrets file.
93	
94	```ts
95	(params: { key: string; value: string }) => { ok: true }
96	```
97	
98	### `secrets.delete`
99	
100	Removes a secret from the plugin's encrypted secrets file.
101	
102	```ts
103	(params: { key: string }) => { ok: true }
104	```
105	
106	### `settings.get`
107	
108	Reads every setting the plugin owns.
109	
110	```ts
111	(params: {}) => { settings: Record<string, JSON> }
112	```
113	
114	### `settings.set`
115	
116	Writes one setting the plugin owns.
117	
118	```ts
119	(params: { key: string; value: JSON }) => { ok: true }
120	```
121	
122	## Errors
123	
124	A failed call rejects with an `Error` carrying `code`, `message`, `retryable` and, for `rate_limited`, `retryAfterMs`. Treat a code not listed here as `action_failed`:
125	
126	- `invalid_request`: the call itself is malformed.
127	- `invalid_params`: params do not match the method, including a field this Orca does not know; the message names it.
128	- `unknown_method`: the method does not exist in this Orca.
129	- `capability_denied`: the manifest does not declare the capability.
130	- `consent_required`: the plugin is disabled or the user has not approved this version.
131	- `not_permitted`: the method or document is not available here, e.g. a worker-only method from a panel.
132	- `rate_limited`: calls arrive faster than the budget; `retryAfterMs` says when to try again.
133	- `unavailable`: the service behind the method is not running yet.
134	- `action_failed`: the method ran and failed.
135	- `cancelled`: the caller aborted the call through its `signal`.
136	- `timeout`: Orca gave up waiting.
137	- `conflict`: the call was made against a stale version, e.g. an editor edit after an outside change.
138	- `too_large`: the message is larger than Orca accepts.
139	
140	## Stability and deprecation
141	
142	Plugins are in Alpha: the manifest v2 format and catalog format are stable contracts; items listed as experimental in [Plugin authoring](./plugin-authoring.md#stability) may change.
143	
144	- **Host API 1 is frozen.** Within `pluginApi` 1, methods, params and results only grow: a new method or a new optional param arrives with a higher `Since` minor, and nothing listed here is removed, renamed or narrowed.
145	- **Deprecation.** A method to be retired is marked deprecated in this table and keeps working for the rest of the major.
146	- **New majors.** A breaking change ships as a new `pluginApi` major beside the old one. Orca refuses a manifest whose `pluginApi` names a major it does not implement, with "update Orca", instead of loading it against the wrong API.
147	- **Detect, do not assume.** Check `orca.host.has(name)` or `orca.api.minor` before calling a method newer than the oldest Orca you support; a call that slips through fails with `unknown_method`.
